solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Following delay of months, slander hospital department’s union (9)

indicators.note: the M for months is held back and arrives after the rest of MALIGN

blocks.note: MALIGN = slander, with its M (months) moved to the end
ENT = ear, nose and throat department

annotation.surface: A hospital department, kept waiting for months, is smeared in the press.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's on department's is the verb 'is': the whole of the wordplay IS union. M for months is a standard abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: An alignment is a union or alliance, as of political parties.

entries.clue: Fools judge? Not quite (5)

indicators.note: not quite all of the word: its last letter goes

blocks.note: a six-letter verb for judge or evaluate, stopped one letter short

annotation.surface: A sneer at the bench: judges are fools, or nearly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Judge' looks like a noun, a person on the bench, which fits the insult; it is the verb, to assess, docked its last S.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the donkey's name has long been the everyday word for a stupid person.

entries.clue: People from Indiana share twin sons (11)

blocks.note: IN is the postal abbreviation for Indiana
a divi is a dividend, a share of profits
twin = dual, as in twin/dual controls
s = son(s), from genealogies

annotation.surface: Hoosiers split the family estate between twin boys.
annotation.walkthrough: 'People from Indiana' reads as one phrase; the definition is only 'People', and 'from' belongs to it as the link. Divi is a British shortening of dividend.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: persons counted singly, as in 'three people' or 'three separate persons'.

entries.clue: Head of state no longer in charge following union of cardinals (7)

indicators.note: to follow is to come after, so the head of state and 'in charge' are placed after the union

blocks.note: NUM = National Union of Mineworkers
ER = Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen
i/c = in charge

annotation.surface: A ruler loses power after the college of cardinals unites, a papal conclave scene.
annotation.walkthrough: The cardinals are not churchmen but cardinal numbers (one, two, three). The NUM is the British coal miners' union.
annotation.definitionFit: Cardinal numbers are numeric, so 'of cardinals' describes something numeric.

entries.clue: Defective electronic chip’s core codes formed imitative words (8)

indicators.note: a faulty set of letters is to be rebuilt
the core of CHIP is its middle, HI

blocks.note: e- = electronic, as in e-mail
the middle two letters of CHIP
taken as written

annotation.surface: A faulty chip scrambles its codes into gibberish noises.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole verb phrase: to echoise is to make words that imitate sounds, like 'buzz'.
annotation.definitionFit: A dictionary sense: to echoise is to coin onomatopoeic words, those that mimic the sound they name.

entries.clue: Breaking in, tense street urchin lowering head (6)

indicators.note: in a down answer, the head (first letter) of GAMIN drops to the bottom

blocks.note: t = tense, in grammar
GAMIN = street urchin, its G moved to the end

annotation.surface: A nervous street kid breaks into a house, keeping his head down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Breaking in' looks like burglary; it is breaking in a horse.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from horsemanship: a wild horse is broken in by being made docile and trained to the saddle.

entries.clue: Public school lodge reported (5)

indicators.note: what is reported is heard, not read

blocks.note: to lodge something is to stow it

annotation.surface: A news item about a public school's lodge.
annotation.walkthrough: Stowe is a well-known English boarding school; in Britain 'public school' means a private fee-paying one.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: one of the famous fee-paying boarding schools, in Buckinghamshire.

entries.clue: Hurt forces brought up case for three days (7)

indicators.note: in a down answer, what is brought up reads bottom to top
the case of a word is its outside pair of letters

blocks.note: RAMS = forces, turned upward
the outer letters of THREE
d = day(s)

annotation.surface: Wounded troops are carried up in a stretcher-case, three days on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Forces' looks like a noun, the armed forces; it is the verb, as in rams home. 'Case for three days' is split: the case holds only 'three', and 'days' stands alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Hurt as a past-tense verb: it smarted, it stung.

entries.clue: Old newspaper much of the time in verse? (3)

annotation.definition: much of the time in verse

blocks.note: o = old
FT = the Financial Times

annotation.surface: A defunct paper that ran poetry most days.
annotation.walkthrough: The FT is the Financial Times, a British daily. 'Oft' is the poets' word for often.
annotation.definitionFit: Oft is a poetic word for often, much of the time.

entries.clue: Continental jargon primarily used in sensitive, regressive summit (9)

indicators.note: take the first letter of 'used'
that U goes inside the next word
regressing, the word runs backwards

blocks.note: first letter
SORE = sensitive, turned round; U goes in after its E
a peak is a summit

annotation.surface: Jargon at a touchy EU summit that is going backwards.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Continental' is British for mainland European; the answer is the jargon of EU officialdom.
annotation.definitionFit: Eurospeak is the jargon of the European Union's institutions.

entries.clue: Depraved scene from “love party” embodied by aggressive-submissive proclivity (5)

indicators.note: OD O sits inside the body of S M

blocks.note: S&M, sadomasochism
love = nil = O, in tennis
a do is a party

annotation.surface: A racy orgy description, the kind of scene a tabloid would relish.
annotation.walkthrough: S&M is sadomasochism, the 'aggressive-submissive proclivity', reduced to its two initials, which then wrap around the love and the party.
annotation.definitionFit: Sodom, the Biblical city, is the byword for a depraved place.

entries.clue: Second-rate artiste carrying more weight on thigh (9)

indicators.note: in an across answer, FATTER is placed on (after) HAM

blocks.note: the ham is the back of the thigh
fatter = heavier

annotation.surface: A mediocre performer putting weight on around the thighs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second-rate artiste' suggests HAM, which the answer does contain, but the ham in the wordplay is the thigh.
annotation.definitionFit: A hamfatter is an old term for an incompetent, ranting actor.

entries.clue: Monarchies asserting vetoes abroad (9,6)

indicators.note: scattered widely, so the letters are shuffled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters

annotation.surface: Kingdoms flexing their veto rights in foreign affairs.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: independent countries need not have kings, but a monarchy is literally a nation ruled by a sovereign, which is the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun on sovereign: a king or queen is a sovereign, so a kingdom is read as a nation belonging to one.

entries.clue: Film of Charles upset Diana briefly (3,4,3,1)

indicators.note: knocked over, so the letters are rearranged
cut short: DIANA loses its last letter

blocks.note: Charles III is the king
DIAN(a) rearranged

annotation.surface: A royal biopic about Charles that upset Diana.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is royal gossip; the answer is the Rodgers and Hammerstein musical film about a king of Siam.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the 1956 Rodgers and Hammerstein musical starring Yul Brynner.

entries.clue: Took away cover from discharge pipe examined at both ends (8)

indicators.note: the cover of a word is its outside letters
keep only the first and last letters

blocks.note: D and E, the outside of DISCHARGE
a duct is a pipe
E and D, the ends of EXAMINED

annotation.surface: A plumber removes the cover of a waste pipe and inspects both ends.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Took away cover' reads as one action; the definition stops at 'Took away', as in subtraction.
annotation.definitionFit: Deducted means took away, as a sum from a total.

entries.clue: Dry ditty regularly confused with 14 (9)

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so the letters are taken at a steady step, every other one
mixed up together, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: D, T, Y: the odd letters of DITTY
the answer to 14 across

annotation.surface: A dull little song muddled up with some other item.
annotation.walkthrough: A number in a clue stands for the answer at that number, here ADHERE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to remove all the water from something, as with dried fruit.

entries.clue: Stick notice in The Times? (6)

blocks.note: an ad is a notice
the clue is printed in The Times, so 'in The Times' is here

annotation.surface: Posting a notice in the paper.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the self-reference: this very puzzle is in The Times, so its location is HERE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: glue makes things stick, cling fast to a surface.

entries.clue: Scold Henry in school, location of Maggie’s education (8)

indicators.note: 'in school' puts the scolding and Henry inside the school, as a pupil sits in one

blocks.note: to rant is to scold loudly
H = henry, the unit of inductance
a gam is a school of whales

annotation.surface: A teacher tells off a pupil called Henry at school.
annotation.walkthrough: Maggie is Margaret Thatcher, who grew up and went to school in Grantham, a Lincolnshire town.
annotation.definitionFit: Grantham is where Margaret Thatcher was born and educated.

entries.clue: Catch securing edges of door-plate in tank (6)

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so the catch word holds the door's edges inside it
take the two outside letters

blocks.note: to catch what is said is to hear it
D and E, the outside of DOOR-PLATE

annotation.surface: A latch fixing a door-plate on some sort of tank.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Catch' looks like the definition, a fastener; it is the verb hear. A header is the raised tank feeding a plumbing system.
annotation.definitionFit: A header, short for header tank, is a tank that feeds water by gravity.

entries.clue: Met maker of saw that’s turned up in River Dee (7)

indicators.note: in a down answer, turned up reads bottom to top
the reversed saw sits in the river, placed inside its name

blocks.note: to rip is to saw along the grain, as with a ripsaw
the Exe, a river in Devon
dee is the name of the letter D

annotation.surface: A saw manufacturer who turned up on the River Dee.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Met maker' is short for met one's maker, died. 'River Dee' looks like one name, but Dee is the spelt-out letter D.
annotation.definitionFit: To expire is to die, to meet one's maker.

entries.clue: Good buzz surrounding Polish play in Rugby (4,4)

indicators.note: to surround is to enclose, so 'good buzz' is wrapped around the polish

blocks.note: g = good
to polish is to rub
a kick is a thrill, a buzz

annotation.surface: A Polish player gives a good buzz to a rugby match.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital on Polish is disguise: it is the verb polish. A grub kick is a low kick along the ground in rugby.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a low punt that skids along the ground, one kicking option in rugby.

entries.clue: Incorporate legal draft delivered prior to crash (5,2)

indicators.note: a speech is delivered, so this is spoken
prior means earlier, so the spoken bill is placed ahead of the crash

blocks.note: a bill is a draft law; BUIL in 'build' sounds exactly like it
a crash is a din, a loud noise

annotation.surface: A draft law passed just before a financial crash.
annotation.walkthrough: The spoken piece is not a whole word: only the first four letters of the answer are voiced as the draft law, and the enumeration break falls elsewhere.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a builder makes a fitted wardrobe part of the wall, incorporating it into the structure.

entries.clue: Fat cat completely extra (2-4)

blocks.note: a nob is a toff, a wealthy person
all = completely, as in all alone

annotation.surface: A plutocrat who is completely surplus to requirements.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket, a no-ball is an illegal delivery, and the run it gives away counts as an extra.
annotation.definitionFit: A no-ball is one kind of extra in cricket scoring.

entries.clue: Regrettably, couple that initiates divorce furtive about settling (15)

indicators.note: the pair of letters that start DIVORCE
SLY goes around APPOINTING

blocks.note: the first two letters of DIVORCE
sly = furtive
settling a date is appointing it

annotation.surface: A couple, sadly, start a divorce while being sneaky about the settlement.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Couple' and 'settling' pull towards marriage and divorce settlements; the couple is two letters and settling is fixing a time.
annotation.definitionFit: Disappointingly is a sentence adverb meaning regrettably.

entries.clue: Second person finally seen collecting litter? (5)

indicators.note: take the last letter of each of the next words

blocks.note: 'you' is the second-person pronoun
the last letters of SEEN and COLLECTING

annotation.surface: Another person is spotted picking up rubbish.
annotation.walkthrough: The litter is not rubbish but a litter of pups or kittens; the question mark admits the definition is by example.
annotation.definitionFit: A litter is an animal's young, born together.

entries.clue: Bizarre dream, not the first that involves intro to Finnegans Wake (9)

indicators.note: weird, so the letters are rearranged
DREAM loses its first letter
the first letter of FINNEGANS

blocks.note: DREAM without its D
taken as written
first letter

annotation.surface: A bizarre dream, which Joyce's Finnegans Wake famously is.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Finnegans Wake' reads as the book title, but 'Wake' is split off as the definition, meaning the aftermath of something.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative synonym: the wake is the trail a ship leaves behind, so what follows in the wake of an event is its consequences.

entries.clue: Leading trio to sign letter overseas (3)

indicators.note: take the first three letters

blocks.note: the first three letters of TAURUS, a sign of the zodiac

annotation.surface: Three leaders sign a letter abroad.
annotation.walkthrough: The sign must be found before its first three letters can be taken; 'overseas' marks the letter as foreign, here Greek.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Greek equivalent of T, a letter used abroad.

entries.clue: London authority protects river for locals (5)

indicators.note: the two words hold the answer inside them

blocks.note: lonDON AUthority

annotation.surface: London's governing body shields a river for its residents.
annotation.walkthrough: The locals are German and Austrian speakers: Donau is their name for the Danube, not a London river.
annotation.definitionFit: Donau is the German name for the Danube, the river as locals call it.

entries.clue: Horse bet, essentially £1 (5)

indicators.note: the essence of BET is its middle letter

blocks.note: middle letter of BET
a quid is British slang for a pound

annotation.surface: A one-pound flutter on a horse.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Horse bet' reads as a single phrase, but the definition is only 'Horse'; the bet gives its middle letter.
annotation.definitionFit: An equid is any member of the horse family.

entries.clue: Soldiers charging Roman Catholic gathering ultimately feeling sorrow (9)

indicators.note: the soldiers are loaded into LATIN, as a charge into a gun
take the last letter of GATHERING

blocks.note: men = soldiers, other ranks
the Latin rite is the Roman Catholic Church's
last letter

annotation.surface: Troops storm a Catholic assembly, and grief follows.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Roman Catholic gathering' looks like one phrase, a Mass; 'gathering' only supplies its last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to mourn aloud, grieving over a loss.
